title: Automate enquiry follow-up so no quote goes quiet
h1: How to automate enquiry follow-up without losing the personal touch
desc: Enquiry follow-up can be automated: a system reads the inbox, quotes and invoices, finds what went quiet and drafts replies a person approves before sending.
lead: Enquiry follow-up can be automated by a system that reads the inbox, the quotes and the invoices, finds every conversation that went quiet, and drafts the next reply. A person reads each draft and approves it, and only then is it sent. Nothing slips, and nothing goes out that the team has not seen.
short: Most lost work is not refused, it simply goes quiet.
The system reads the inbox, quotes and invoices and lists what has had no reply.
It drafts each follow-up in the firm's own voice, with the context attached.
A person approves every message before it is sent.

sections.h2: Why do enquiries and quotes go quiet?
body: An enquiry arrives on a busy day. Someone answers it, sends a quote, and means to check back later. Then other work comes in, and the thread sinks below newer messages. Nobody decided to drop it. It was simply nobody's job to look again.

The same thing happens in firms of every size, from an independent professional to an established firm with a shared inbox. The more people share an inbox, the easier it is for each to assume someone else is chasing. The cost is quiet: work the firm was close to winning, lost without a no.
Follow-up is a chore that depends on memory. That makes it a good candidate for a system, as long as the system does the remembering and the drafting, and a person keeps the final word.

sections.h2: What does an automated follow-up system actually do?
body: The system Loose Ends builds works inside the tools the firm already uses. It does not replace the inbox or the accounting tool. It reads them and keeps a list of what needs attention.
Reads the inbox for enquiries and the replies to them.
Reads sent quotes and open invoices, so it knows what was offered and what is still unpaid.
Finds every conversation where the last message came from the firm and nothing came back.
Drafts a follow-up for each one, referring to what was actually discussed.
Places the drafts in a queue for a person to read, edit, approve or discard.
Sends only what was approved, from the firm's own address.
The result is a short list each morning instead of a search through old threads. The team stops retyping the same chasing email and starts reviewing ready drafts.

sections.h2: How does the system decide what has gone quiet?
body: The firm sets the rules, in plain terms, during the build. A rule might say that a quote with no reply after a set number of days should be followed up, or that an enquiry answered once and never acknowledged should be checked again.

Different kinds of work can have different rules. A large proposal may deserve a longer pause than a quick price question. A returning client may get a warmer note than a first enquiry. The rules sit in one place, so changing them later does not mean rebuilding anything.
The system also knows when to stop. If the client replied, booked, paid or said no, the thread leaves the list. That keeps the queue honest and stops anyone being chased twice.

sections.h2: Who approves the follow-up before it is sent?
body: A named person on the team approves each message. This is a design rule in every system Loose Ends builds: the system drafts and prepares, and a person approves before anything reaches a client.

Approval is quick when the draft is good. The person sees the original enquiry, the quote, the date of the last message and the proposed reply on one screen. They can send it as it is, change a line, or decide the thread should rest.

This step matters for more than safety. A follow-up is part of the relationship. The person approving it may know that the client is travelling, or that a phone call would be better. The system cannot know that, so it does not pretend to.

sections.h2: What does a good follow-up draft look like?
body: A useful draft is short, specific and written in the firm's own tone. It refers to the actual work discussed, not to a template placeholder. It asks one clear question that is easy to answer.
It names the quote or the request it refers to.
It restates the one detail the client is most likely to need.
It offers a simple next step, such as a time to talk or a yes or no.
It sounds like the person who wrote the first message.
During the build, the studio collects examples of how the team already writes, so the drafts match. If a draft reads wrong, the person approving it corrects it, and the examples can be updated.

A draft should also know what not to say. It does not invent a discount, promise a date the team has not agreed, or guess at a detail missing from the thread. Where something is unclear, the draft leaves a note for the person approving it instead of filling the gap.

sections.h2: Which tools can it connect to?
body: The system connects to email, calendar, spreadsheets and the firm's accounting or quoting tool. Where a Claude connector exists, it uses one. Claude connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. Where no connector exists, Loose Ends writes a custom connection to the tool's API.
The firm keeps ownership of everything: the code, the accounts and the data. The build is agreed at one fixed price in writing, and at handover every routine has a named owner on the team.

The approval queue can sit wherever the team already works. For some firms that is the inbox itself, with drafts waiting in a folder. For others it is a Slack channel or a simple internal page. The aim is that approving a follow-up takes no more effort than reading an email.

sections.h2: Where should a firm start?
body: The simplest start is to list where enquiries and quotes arrive and who is expected to chase them. That alone often shows where things go quiet. From there, a paid audit can rank the first fixes, with the fee credited toward the build. To see where follow-up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Does automated follow-up send emails on its own?
faq.a: No. The system drafts each follow-up and places it in a queue. A person approves it before it is sent.

faq.q: Can it follow up on quotes as well as enquiries?
faq.a: Yes. It reads sent quotes and open invoices alongside the inbox, so it can find a quote with no reply as easily as an unanswered enquiry.

faq.q: Will the messages sound like a template?
faq.a: The drafts are written from the actual thread and from examples of how the team already writes. The person approving can change any line before it goes.

faq.q: Does the firm have to change its email or accounting tool?
faq.a: No. The system works inside the tools the firm already uses and connects to them through connectors or custom API connections.

title: Automate invoice reminders with a person approving each one
h1: How to automate invoice reminders and keep the tone right
desc: Invoice reminders can run on a schedule: the system checks the accounting tool, drafts a reminder for each stage, and a person approves it before it is sent.
lead: Invoice reminders can be automated by connecting the accounting tool to email and letting a system check, on a schedule, which invoices are due or overdue. At each stage it drafts a reminder in the right tone, and a person approves it before it is sent. The chasing happens on time, and nobody has to remember it.
short: The system checks open invoices on a set schedule.
Each stage has its own tone, from a friendly note to a firmer request.
A person approves every reminder before it reaches a client.
Paid invoices drop off the list on their own.

sections.h2: Why is chasing invoices so easy to put off?
body: Chasing an unpaid invoice is uncomfortable. It interrupts other work, it means opening the accounting tool, finding the invoice, checking whether it was already chased, and writing an email that is polite but clear. It is the kind of chore that waits until the end of the month.

By then, several invoices may be late at once, and the reminders go out in a rush with an uneven tone. Some clients get chased twice. Others are missed. The firm's cash arrives later than it should, and the relationship gets an awkward edge it did not need.

The problem is rarely that nobody cares. It is that chasing depends on someone remembering to look, at the right moment, in a tool they do not open every day. That is exactly the kind of work a scheduled system does well, provided a person still decides what is sent.

sections.h2: How does scheduled invoice follow-up work?
body: The system Loose Ends builds reads the firm's accounting tool on a regular schedule. It looks at every open invoice, its due date and its history of reminders. It then decides which ones need a message today and drafts that message.
Checks open invoices and their due dates on a set schedule.
Works out which stage each invoice has reached.
Drafts the reminder for that stage, with the invoice number, amount and a link to pay.
Places each draft in a queue for a person to approve, edit or hold.
Sends the approved reminders from the firm's own email address.
Records what was sent, so the next stage starts from the right point.
When the accounting tool shows an invoice as paid, it leaves the list. Nobody receives a reminder for something they already settled.

sections.h2: What stages should invoice reminders follow?
body: The firm decides the stages and the timing during the build. A common pattern is a gentle note shortly before the due date, a polite reminder soon after it, a clearer request if the invoice stays unpaid, and finally a message that hands the matter to a named person on the team.

Each stage has its own wording. Early messages assume an oversight. Later ones are more direct about dates and next steps. The last stage does not threaten anything on its own: it brings a person in, because a long overdue invoice usually needs a conversation, not another email.
The stages are kept in one place, so they can be changed without rebuilding the system.

Each reminder also carries the facts the client needs to act straight away: the invoice number, the amount, the original due date, and a way to pay. A clear reminder is answered sooner than a vague one, and it saves the client from writing back to ask which invoice is meant.

sections.h2: How is the tone kept right for each client?
body: Not every client should be chased the same way. A long-standing client with one late invoice deserves different words from an account that is often late. The system can hold notes for each client, such as a preferred contact, a known payment cycle or a request to always copy someone in accounts.
A preferred contact name for each client.
The client's usual payment pattern, so the timing fits.
Accounts that should always be handled by a person, never drafted.
Phrases the firm uses, and phrases it never uses.
The person approving each reminder sees these notes beside the draft. If something feels wrong, they change it or hold it.

sections.h2: Why does a person approve every reminder?
body: A reminder about money touches the relationship directly. The system can see dates and amounts, but it cannot see that the client called yesterday to say payment is on its way, or that a dispute is open. A person can.

That is why every system Loose Ends builds drafts first and waits for approval before anything reaches a client. Approval takes a moment when the draft is right, and it catches the cases where sending would be a mistake. The team still decides; it just no longer has to remember.

The approval queue can be set up where the team already works. Some firms prefer a daily email listing the reminders waiting, with a button to approve each one. Others prefer a Slack channel or a short page inside an internal tool. In every case, the person sees the invoice, its history and the draft together, so the decision takes a moment.

sections.h2: Which accounting and email tools can it connect to?
body: The system connects to the firm's accounting or invoicing tool, its email and, where useful, a spreadsheet or a Slack channel where the approval queue appears. Where a Claude connector exists, the studio uses it. Connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024. Where none exists, Loose Ends builds a custom connection to the tool's API.
The code, the accounts and the data belong to the firm. At handover, the team is trained, and a named person owns the routine.
The same connection can also feed a short weekly view of what is outstanding, so the team sees at a glance which invoices are waiting and which reminders were sent.

sections.h2: How should a firm get started?
body: A good first step is to write down how invoices are chased today: who does it, when and with what wording. The gaps usually show up straight away. A paid audit can then rank the first fixes, with the fee credited toward a build at one fixed price. To see where follow-up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Will clients receive reminders automatically without anyone checking?
faq.a: No. Each reminder is drafted and queued. A person approves it before it is sent.

faq.q: What happens when a client pays?
faq.a: The system reads the accounting tool, so once an invoice is marked as paid it leaves the list and no further reminders are drafted.
Yes. Any client can be marked to be handled only by a person, and the system will flag their invoices without drafting a reminder.

title: Booking confirmation and reminder automation, explained
h1: How to automate booking confirmations, reminders and rescheduling
desc: Booking confirmations, reminders and rescheduling can run on their own once bookings live in one place instead of direct messages. Here is how it works.
lead: Booking confirmations, reminders and rescheduling can be automated once every booking lives in one place, instead of spread across direct messages, emails and a paper diary. The booking system confirms each place, sends a reminder before the session and lets the client move or cancel through a link. The team stops answering, confirming and rescheduling by hand.
short: Bookings first need to leave direct messages and sit in one place.
Confirmations and reminders then go out on their own, from set wording.
Clients reschedule through a link, within rules the business sets.
Anything unusual goes to a person, who decides.

sections.h2: Why do bookings through direct messages cause problems?
body: Many businesses start taking bookings wherever clients write to them: Instagram, WhatsApp, email, a phone call. It works at first. Then someone has to read every message, reply, check the diary, confirm, and remember to remind.

Messages get missed, places are double counted, and the person answering spends evenings confirming instead of working. Payment is chased separately. Rescheduling is another round of messages. None of it is difficult, but all of it is manual, and it falls on whoever has the phone.

Clients notice too. A booking that depends on a reply can wait hours for a confirmation, and a client who is not sure they have a place may book elsewhere. A clear, immediate confirmation is part of good service, not only a saving for the team.

sections.h2: What can booking automation handle on its own?
body: Once bookings sit in one system, most of the routine messages can be sent without anyone typing them. These are factual messages with set wording, approved once by the business.
A confirmation as soon as a place is booked and paid.
A reminder before the session, with the time, place and anything to bring.
A link to reschedule or cancel, within the rules the business sets.
A notice to the next person on a waiting list when a place opens.
An update to the team's calendar or schedule each time something changes.
Because the wording of each message is written and approved by a person once, at setup, these routine notices can go out on their own. Anything that is not routine is handled differently.

Each message should carry only what the client needs: the session, the date and time, the address, what to bring and how to change the booking. Short, factual notices are read, and they cut down the questions that would otherwise come back as more messages to answer.

sections.h2: What should stay with a person?
body: Some booking messages are not routine. A complaint, a request for a refund outside the rules, a question about health or access, or a group booking with special terms all need a human answer.

The system flags these and drafts a reply where it can, but a person approves it before it reaches the client. This follows the rule Loose Ends applies everywhere: the system prepares, and a person approves anything that is not a fixed, pre-approved notice.
It also matters for the tone of the business. A reminder can be automatic. An apology should not be.

Each flagged message arrives with the booking, the client's history and a suggested reply on one screen. The person deciding reads, adjusts and sends, without searching through old conversations to understand what happened.

sections.h2: How did a yoga studio move its bookings out of Instagram?
body: A yoga studio was taking bookings through Instagram messages. Loose Ends built a booking application that puts the schedule, the available places and payment on a single phone screen, in French and English.

Clients now see the classes, choose a place and pay in one step, without writing a message. Bookings moved out of Instagram messages into one place, where the studio can see who is coming to each class. The application is live.
The point was not to remove contact with clients. It was to stop the studio's messages from being used as a booking diary, so conversations there can be about practice, not about places.
Working in two languages was part of the brief from the start. Clients choose French or English, and the schedule, the confirmation and the payment step follow in that language.

sections.h2: How does rescheduling work without back-and-forth?
body: Rescheduling is where manual booking takes the most time. Each change can mean several messages to find a new slot. With one booking system, the client opens a link, sees what is available and moves the booking, within the limits the business has set.
How close to the session a booking can still be moved.
Whether a late cancellation keeps or releases the payment.
How many times one booking can be moved.
Which sessions can only be changed by a person.
When a change falls outside these rules, the system sends it to the team instead of deciding.

When a place is released, it can be offered to a waiting list straight away. The next person receives a notice and a link, and the class fills again without the team writing to anyone. If nobody takes the place, it simply returns to the public schedule.

sections.h2: Which tools does a booking system connect to?
body: A booking application can connect to the business's calendar, its payment provider, its email and, where useful, a spreadsheet the team already uses for planning. It can also sit inside an existing website. Loose Ends builds the application to order, or connects existing tools where they already do the job.
The code, the domain and the accounts belong to the business, and the build is agreed at one fixed price in writing.

At handover, the team is trained on the system and a named person owns each routine, from the reminder wording to the rescheduling rules. Changes after launch, such as a new class or a new cancellation policy, are made in one place and apply everywhere.

sections.h2: Where should a business begin?
body: Start by listing every place a booking can arrive today and every message the team sends about it. That list is usually longer than expected, and it shows what can be fixed first. To see where follow-up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Do clients need to download an app to book?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A booking application can open in the phone's browser from a link, so clients book on a single screen without installing anything.

faq.q: Can confirmations and reminders be sent automatically?
faq.a: Yes. Their wording is written and approved by a person once, at setup. Messages that are not routine, such as replies to complaints, are drafted and approved by a person before they are sent.

faq.q: Can the booking system work in more than one language?
faq.a: Yes. The yoga studio's booking application, for example, works in French and English.

faq.q: What if a client wants to reschedule outside the rules?
faq.a: The request goes to a person on the team, who decides and replies.

title: Human-in-the-loop automation: approve before it sends
h1: Human-in-the-loop automation: why every system should draft first
desc: Human-in-the-loop automation means the system drafts and a person approves before anything reaches a client. Where approval sits, and what never to automate.
lead: Human-in-the-loop automation means the system does the reading, sorting and drafting, and a person approves before anything reaches a client. It keeps the time saved by automation and removes the risk of a wrong message going out under the firm's name. Loose Ends builds every system this way.
short: The system prepares; a person approves anything a client will see.
Internal chores can often run fully on their own.
Some decisions should never be automated, whatever the tool.
Approval is also how mistakes are caught and the system improves.

sections.h2: What does human-in-the-loop automation mean?
body: It means a person stays in the process at the point where it matters. The system does the work that takes time: reading the inbox, finding what needs attention, pulling figures, drafting the reply. A person then reads the result and decides whether it goes.

This is different from automation that runs end to end with no review. That kind of automation is fine for some jobs and wrong for others. The question is not whether to automate, but where to put the person.

In practice, most of the time in a routine goes into finding and preparing, not into the final decision. A person can approve a ready reply in moments, but finding the thread, checking the quote and writing the reply from scratch takes far longer. Human-in-the-loop automation takes the slow part away and leaves the decision where it was.

sections.h2: Why should a system draft first instead of sending?
body: Anything sent to a client speaks for the firm. A system can read the facts in front of it, but it cannot know everything the team knows: that a client called this morning, that a project is sensitive, that a phrase will land badly.

Drafting first keeps the speed of automation without handing over the firm's voice. The person approving does not start from a blank page. They read, adjust and send. When the draft is good, approval takes a moment. When it is not, the mistake stops there.
It also makes the system easier to trust. A team that sees every draft for the first weeks learns quickly what the system does well, and where it needs better rules.

sections.h2: Where should the approval step sit?
body: Approval should sit at the last point before something leaves the firm, and nowhere else it is not needed. Too many approval steps and the team stops reading them. Too few and something slips through.
Before any email, message or document is sent to a client.
Before anything is published under the firm's name, such as a post or an article.
Before money moves, such as a refund or a payment run.
Before a record is changed in a way that is hard to undo.
The approval screen should show everything needed to decide: the original message, the context the system used, and the draft. A person should never have to open several tools to approve one reply.

The queue itself can live wherever the team already works: in the inbox as a folder of drafts, in a Slack channel, or on a simple internal page. What matters is that it is checked at a set time each day, and that one named person is responsible for it.

sections.h2: What can be automated fully?
body: Work that stays inside the firm and can be checked later is usually safe to run on its own. Copying data from one tool to another, filing documents into the right folder, preparing a weekly figures summary for the team, or adding a new booking to the calendar are good examples.

Fixed notices whose wording a person has already approved, such as a booking confirmation or a reminder before a session, can also go out on their own. The approval happened once, at setup, and the message does not change.

A useful test is to ask what happens if the system gets it wrong. If the answer is that someone on the team notices and fixes it with no harm done, the job can usually run on its own. If the answer is that a client receives something wrong, or money moves, a person approves first.

sections.h2: What should never be automated?
body: Some decisions belong to people, however good the tools become. Loose Ends does not build systems that make these on their own.
Hiring decisions. In Vero, the studio's own recruiting software, the system ranks candidates and shows its reasoning, but the decision stays with the recruiter.
Replies to complaints, disputes or anything sensitive.
Changes to prices, terms or contracts.
Anything that fills a gap in the facts with a guess.

On the last point, the studio's systems are built to flag a gap rather than fill it. A report built from interview notes, for example, points every rating to its source and marks what is missing, instead of inventing it.

The same applies to Loose Ends' own scoring product, ZonedInOut. It scores stocks, funds and cryptocurrencies each trading day and publishes and grades its past calls, but it is a scoring system, not financial advice. The decision to act stays with the person.

sections.h2: How are mistakes caught?
body: The approval step catches most mistakes before they matter. The rest of the design makes them easier to see. Every draft shows where its facts came from. Every score or rating points to the source text behind it. Every message sent is recorded, so the team can look back.

When a person changes a draft, that change is useful information. If the same correction keeps coming up, the rules or examples behind the drafts are updated. Over time, the drafts need fewer changes, and the approval step stays quick.
At handover, every routine has a named owner on the team, so there is always one person who knows how it works and notices when something looks wrong.

sections.h2: How does a firm decide where to start?
body: List the chores the team repeats each week, then mark which ones send something to a client. Those get a draft and an approval step. The others may run on their own. To see where follow-up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Does human-in-the-loop automation slow things down?
faq.a: Very little, when drafts are good. The person approving reads and sends instead of writing from scratch, and the slow part, finding and preparing, is done by the system.

faq.q: Can some messages go out without approval?
faq.a: Fixed notices whose wording was approved once at setup, such as booking confirmations, can. Anything written for a specific client is approved by a person first.
A named person on the team, agreed at handover. Every routine has an owner, so approvals never fall between people.

title: Automate weekly reporting: figures ready before anyone asks
h1: How to automate weekly reporting from the tools a firm already uses
desc: Weekly reporting can be automated by pulling figures from existing tools into one dashboard and sending the team a short summary in Slack or email each week.
lead: Weekly reporting can be automated by connecting the tools that already hold the figures, gathering them into one dashboard, and sending the team a short written summary on a set day. The numbers are ready before anyone asks for them. Nobody spends the morning copying figures between tabs.
short: Figures are pulled from the tools the firm already uses.
One dashboard shows them in the same place every week.
A short summary goes to the team in Slack or by email.
Gaps and odd figures are flagged, never filled with a guess.

sections.h2: Why does weekly reporting take so long?
body: The figures a team needs each week usually live in several places: sales in one tool, bookings in another, invoices in the accounting system, enquiries in the inbox, campaign results somewhere else. Someone opens each one, copies the numbers into a spreadsheet, checks them and writes a few lines about what changed.
It is retyping work. It is easy to get a figure wrong, and it often happens late, after someone has asked. When the person who usually does it is away, the report is skipped.

The result is a meeting that starts with questions about the numbers rather than about what to do. Time goes into finding figures instead of reading them. The work is necessary, but the copying part of it does not need a person.

sections.h2: What does automated weekly reporting look like?
body: The system Loose Ends builds connects to each source, collects the agreed figures on a schedule and places them in one dashboard. It then writes a short summary of what moved and sends it to the team.
Reads figures from each connected tool on a set day and time.
Stores them, so each week can be compared with the last.
Updates a single dashboard the whole team can open.
Writes a short summary of what changed and what needs a look.
Sends the summary to a Slack channel or by email.
Flags any figure that is missing or out of the usual range.
The dashboard and the summary are built around the questions the team actually asks each week, not around every number the tools can produce.

Because the figures are collected the same way every week, they can be compared fairly. A change shows up as a change in the business, not as a change in who copied the numbers or which filter they used.

sections.h2: Which figures should a weekly report include?
body: Fewer than most teams expect. A weekly report is useful when it can be read in a minute and acted on. The right figures depend on the business, but they usually answer a handful of plain questions.
What came in: new enquiries, bookings or orders.
What went out: quotes sent, invoices issued, work delivered.
What is waiting: unpaid invoices, unanswered enquiries, open tasks.
What changed compared with last week, and why that might be.
During the build, the studio agrees each figure with the team, including exactly where it comes from, so everyone reads it the same way.

The summary is written in plain sentences, not as another table. It might say that enquiries rose compared with last week, that a few invoices passed their due date, and that one figure could not be read. Each line links to the dashboard for anyone who wants the detail.

sections.h2: Which tools can the figures come from?
body: Most tools a firm already uses can provide figures: accounting and invoicing tools, Shopify and Etsy for online shops, booking systems, spreadsheets and databases, email, calendars and recruiting systems such as Loxo. Where a Claude connector exists, the studio uses it. Connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants to tools and data.
Where no connector exists, Loose Ends builds a custom connection to the tool's API. Nothing needs to be replaced, and the firm keeps ownership of the code, the accounts and the data.

sections.h2: Who checks the summary before it is shared?
body: A summary that stays inside the team can usually go out on its own, because it is prepared from the firm's own figures and the team reads it as a starting point. Each figure links back to its source, so anyone can check it.

If the summary is shared outside the firm, for example with a client, a partner or a board, it is drafted and a person approves it before it is sent. That follows the rule in every system the studio builds: a person approves anything that reaches a client.
In both cases, the system never fills a gap with a guess. If a figure could not be read, the summary says so.

Each figure on the dashboard also shows when it was last updated and which tool it came from. That small detail saves a lot of doubt: when a number looks odd, the team can see at once whether the business changed or the source did.

sections.h2: Can the team ask questions about the figures?
body: Yes, if the data is also connected to the team's AI assistant. Once the figures sit in one place, an assistant such as Claude can be connected to them, so a person can ask a plain question and get an answer drawn from the firm's own data.

Setting up AI assistants for a team, connected to its own data, is the studio's main offer. Most teams use only a fraction of what the assistant can do. A weekly report is often a good first place to close that gap.

At handover, the team is trained on the dashboard and the assistant, and a named person owns the weekly routine. If a new figure is needed later, it is added in one place and appears in both the dashboard and the summary.

sections.h2: Where should a firm start?
body: Write down the figures someone already copies by hand each week and where each comes from. That list is the first version of the dashboard, and it often shows which figures nobody actually reads and can be dropped. To see where follow-up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Is new software needed for automated reporting?
faq.a: Usually not. The system reads from the tools the firm already uses and gathers the figures into one dashboard.

faq.q: Can the weekly summary be sent to Slack?
faq.a: Yes. The summary can go to a Slack channel, by email, or both, on a set day each week.

faq.q: What happens if a figure is missing?
faq.a: The summary says the figure could not be read and points to the source. It never fills the gap with an estimate.

faq.q: Is the report sent to clients automatically?
faq.a: No. Anything shared outside the firm is drafted first, and a person approves it before it is sent.
